home.description: Independent reviews of lead generation and cold email tools — Snov.io, Hunter, Apollo and Lusha — with real pricing ranges, credit maths and practical guides.

faq.q: Is this site independent?
faq.a: Yes. Leads Mania is not Snov.io and is not owned by any tool we cover. Some outbound links are affiliate links, which are marked and disclosed, and they never determine what a review concludes.

faq.q: How do you research a tool before reviewing it?
faq.a: We read the provider’s own product and pricing documentation, then cross-check each factual claim against independent third-party reviews. Where credible sources disagree, we publish the range rather than picking the most flattering figure. See our research methodology page for detail.

faq.q: Do you claim to have tested these tools yourself?
faq.a: No. Our reviews are research-based and say so. We do not publish accuracy percentages, ratings or hands-on claims that we have not measured, and we do not fabricate testing.

faq.q: Which tool should I start with?
faq.a: For a solo user or small team wanting discovery, verification and sequencing in one subscription, Snov.io is a reasonable starting point. If you need a very large searchable database choose Apollo.io; for phone numbers choose Lusha; for simple email lookups on a budget choose Hunter.io.

about.title: About Leads Mania
about.description: Leads Mania publishes independent, research-based reviews of lead generation and cold outreach tools, with disclosed affiliate links and cited sources.
about.content:
Leads Mania is an independent publication about lead generation and cold outreach software. We write for people who have to choose a tool with a real budget and then live with the decision — freelancers, small agencies, recruiters and early sales teams.

What we do

We explain what a tool actually does, what it costs once the credit maths is applied, and where it is weak. Comparisons on this site are structured around the factors that change a purchase decision: who pays per seat versus per credit, cost per verified contact, data coverage, and whether the product includes the downstream steps you would otherwise buy separately.

What we do not do

  • We do not pretend to have tested everything. Our reviews are research-based and labelled as such. If we ever publish hands-on testing, it will say so explicitly and describe the method.
  • We do not invent ratings or numbers. No star scores, accuracy percentages or prices are presented as measured by us.
  • We do not hide commercial relationships. Affiliate links are marked and disclosed, and they never decide a verdict.

How we are funded

Some links to tools are affiliate links. If a reader buys through one, we may earn a commission at no extra cost to them. This is the only revenue on the site: no sponsored posts, no paid placements and no paid rankings. Where a tool is the wrong choice for a use case, we say so regardless of commission. Read the full affiliate disclosure.

Corrections

Pricing and feature sets in this category change constantly, and published figures disagree between sources. If you spot something out of date, we would rather hear it than leave it wrong — please use the contact page.

For detail on how each review is assembled, see how we research.

faq.q: Who writes the reviews on this site?
faq.a: Leads Mania is an independent editorial site. Reviews are compiled from provider documentation and cited third-party sources rather than from paid accounts, and each page lists its sources.

faq.q: Does an affiliate relationship affect your verdicts?
faq.a: No. Affiliate links are disclosed and do not determine conclusions. Several pages recommend a non-affiliate tool where it genuinely fits the use case better.

how-we-research.title: How We Research and Review Tools
how-we-research.description: Our review methodology: primary provider documentation, independent cross-checking, how we handle conflicting figures, and what we refuse to publish.
how-we-research.content:
This page explains exactly how a review on this site is produced, so you can judge how much weight to give it. The short version: we read primary documentation, cross-check against independent sources, publish ranges when sources disagree, and never present invented numbers as measurements.

1. Start with primary documentation

For every tool we cover, we begin with the provider's own material: the pricing page, plan and credit documentation, feature pages and help-centre articles. This establishes what the vendor claims and what the plan limits actually are. Vendor claims are treated as claims, not facts.

2. Cross-check against independent sources

Every material factual claim — a price, a credit rule, a database size, an accuracy figure — is checked against at least one independent third-party review or comparison. Sources are linked at the bottom of each page so a reader can repeat the verification. Where only the vendor states something, we attribute it to the vendor.

3. Publish ranges, not the most flattering number

Pricing in this category is genuinely inconsistent between reviewers. Snov.io's 20K tier is published at $149 in one breakdown and $189 in another; Hunter's indexed address count is variously quoted around 107M and 200M. These differences are usually timing, billing terms or different units being counted. Rather than resolving them by preference, we show the range and say why the figures differ.

4. Work the arithmetic ourselves

Headline prices hide the real cost. Because a finished contact typically costs two credits — one to find, one to verify — we divide plan price by half the credit allowance to get a cost per verified lead. That calculation is ours, and we show the working so you can dispute it.

5. Separate what we know from what we assume

We distinguish four kinds of statement, consistently:

  • Documented — stated in provider documentation, attributed.
  • Reported — claimed by an independent third party, cited.
  • Calculated — derived by us from cited inputs, with the method shown.
  • Judgement — our editorial opinion about who a tool suits, clearly framed as opinion.

6. What we refuse to publish

  • Star ratings or scores presented as the result of testing we did not do.
  • Accuracy percentages we have not measured.
  • Publish or update dates that do not reflect real work on the page.
  • Screenshots or interface captures we do not actually have.
  • Testimonials or case studies that are not real and attributable.

That last set is not modesty — it is what Google's spam and structured-data policies require, and it is also the difference between a review a reader can use and one that wastes their time.

7. Updating

This category changes monthly. When a page is revised, the underlying post date changes with it, and pages that rely on pricing carry an explicit warning that figures are approximate and must be confirmed with the provider.

Limitations you should know about

We do not buy seats on every tool, so we cannot report inbox placement, real-world coverage in your niche, or support responsiveness from experience. On any research-based review those questions remain open, and the honest advice is to run your own twenty-prospect test on a free tier before committing to an annual plan.

Corrections policy

If a figure here is wrong, we want to fix it. Report it through the contact page with the page and the claim, and if it is verifiable we will correct it and note the change.

faq.q: Do you test the tools you review?
faq.a: Not currently. Reviews are research-based: provider documentation plus independent third-party sources, all linked on each page. Any future hands-on testing will be explicitly labelled and its method described.

faq.q: Why do you show price ranges instead of exact prices?
faq.a: Because credible sources publish different figures for the same plans, usually due to billing terms or timing. Showing the range and explaining the discrepancy is more honest than picking one number and presenting it as definitive.

faq.q: How can I report an error?
faq.a: Use the contact page and include the page and the specific claim. If the correction is verifiable against a cited source, we will update the page and note what changed.

contact.title: Contact Leads Mania
contact.description: How to reach Leads Mania about corrections, review suggestions, data errors or general editorial questions, and what response to expect.
contact.content:
We read everything sent to us, and corrections are prioritised over everything else.

Reporting a correction

If a price, plan limit or feature description on this site is out of date or wrong, please tell us. Include:

  • The page URL and the exact claim you are questioning.
  • What the current, correct position is.
  • A link to the provider's own page supporting it, if you have one.

Verified corrections are applied and the page is updated.

Suggesting a tool for review

Tell us the tool, what it does differently, and the specific use case it suits. We prioritise tools that readers ask about more than once.

Editorial and affiliate questions

Questions about how we research, or about affiliate relationships, are answered on the methodology page and in the affiliate disclosure. If something is still unclear, ask.

What we do not do

We do not sell guest posts, paid links, "sponsored" reviews or placement in our comparison tables, and we do not accept payment to change a verdict. Requests of that kind are declined.

Contact details: this page is a template placeholder. Replace this paragraph with a real, monitored email address or contact form before publishing — a contact page with no working contact method undermines trust and is a signal reviewers and readers both notice.

faq.q: How quickly do you respond?
faq.a: There is no published response guarantee. Corrections are treated as the highest priority because an inaccurate price is the most damaging thing this site can publish.

faq.q: Can I pay for a review or a link?
faq.a: No. We do not sell guest posts, paid links, sponsored reviews or placement in comparison tables, and we do not accept payment to change a verdict.

affiliate-disclosure.title: Affiliate Disclosure
affiliate-disclosure.description: How Leads Mania uses affiliate links, which links are commercial, how sponsorship is marked, and why commissions do not determine our reviews or verdicts.
affiliate-disclosure.content:
Leads Mania is reader-supported. Some links on this site are affiliate links, which means we may earn a commission if you buy a product through them, at no additional cost to you.

Which links are commercial

Affiliate links point to third-party products, are labelled as such where they appear, and open in a new tab. They carry rel="sponsored nofollow noopener" so that search engines can identify them as commercial links. Editorial links to sources and documentation are not commercial and are marked rel="noopener".

What commission does not buy

  • It does not buy a positive verdict. Where a non-affiliate tool is the better fit for a use case, we say so.
  • It does not buy placement. Comparison tables are ordered by fit, not by commission rate.
  • It does not buy silence about weaknesses. Every tool we cover has a limitations section, and it is not decorative.

What we do not accept

No paid guest posts, no paid links, no sponsored reviews, no payment to alter a conclusion. If that changes, this page will say so before anything else does.

Pricing and accuracy

Prices and plan terms on this site are approximate snapshots compiled from third-party sources and can be out of date. Always confirm current pricing on the provider's own site before purchasing. We are not responsible for a purchase decision made on stale figures.

Independence

Leads Mania is an independent publication. We are not Snov.io, are not owned by Snov.io, and are not affiliated with any provider beyond the commercial link relationships disclosed here. No provider reviews or approves our content before publication.

Questions

If anything about a commercial relationship on this site is unclear, ask through the contact page.

faq.q: Do affiliate commissions affect your reviews?
faq.a: They are not permitted to. Verdicts follow the research, non-affiliate tools are recommended where they fit better, and every review states the tool’s limitations. The only revenue on the site is disclosed affiliate commission.

faq.q: How are affiliate links marked?
faq.a: They are labelled where they appear and carry rel="sponsored nofollow noopener". Editorial links to sources and documentation are separate and not commercial.

privacy-policy.title: Privacy Policy
privacy-policy.description: What data this website processes, how cookies and analytics are used, how affiliate links work, your rights under GDPR and how to exercise them.
privacy-policy.content:
Draft — not legal advice. This policy is a template describing the configuration of this site as built. It must be adapted to your actual hosting, analytics, email and affiliate setup, and reviewed by someone qualified in your jurisdiction before publication.

Who we are

Leads Mania publishes editorial reviews of lead generation software. For the purposes of the EU/UK General Data Protection Regulation, the site operator is the data controller for personal data processed through this website.

What we collect

  • Server logs. Your IP address, browser type, referring page and requested URL are recorded by the hosting provider for security and troubleshooting. These are retained for a limited period.
  • Analytics. If analytics are enabled, aggregate data about page views and referral sources is collected. See the analytics section below.
  • Messages you send us. If you contact us, we hold your message and contact details in order to reply.
  • Cookies. See below.

We do not run signup forms, we do not sell personal data, and we do not build advertising profiles of readers.

Cookies

This site sets no advertising cookies. Strictly necessary cookies may be set by the hosting platform for security and load balancing. If analytics or affiliate networks are added, they may set their own cookies; where consent is legally required for those, it must be requested before they load.

Analytics

No analytics package is currently included in this build. If one is added, this section will name the provider, state whether IP addresses are anonymised, and describe how to opt out. Prefer a privacy-respecting, cookie-light analytics tool; it keeps the consent burden low.

Affiliate links and third parties

Clicking an affiliate link takes you to a third-party site. That provider may set cookies to attribute the referral, and their privacy policy — not ours — governs what happens on their site. We do not receive your personal data from those providers; we may receive aggregate reports showing that a sale occurred.

Legal bases

  • Legitimate interests — operating and securing the website, and understanding aggregate readership.
  • Consent — for any non-essential cookie or analytics tool that requires it.
  • Contract — where we need to correspond with you about something you asked for.

Your rights

Under GDPR you may request access to your personal data, correction of inaccuracies, erasure, restriction of processing, portability, and objection to processing based on legitimate interests. You also have the right to complain to your national supervisory authority. To exercise any right, contact us through the contact page.

Retention

Server logs are kept for a short operational period. Correspondence is kept only as long as needed to resolve the matter, then deleted.

International transfers

Hosting and service providers may process data outside your country. Where required, transfers rely on appropriate safeguards such as standard contractual clauses.

Children

This site is aimed at business users and is not directed at children.

Changes

If this policy changes materially, the change will be reflected on this page with an updated revision.

faq.q: Does this site sell my data?
faq.a: No. There are no signup forms, no advertising profiles and no sale of personal data. The only processing is server logs, any analytics that are enabled, and messages you choose to send.

faq.q: Do affiliate links set cookies?
faq.a: The destination provider may set a cookie to attribute the referral once you click through. That happens on their site and is governed by their privacy policy, not this one.

snov-io-review.title: Snov.io Review 2026: Features, Pricing and Fit
snov-io-review.description: Snov.io review: email finding, verification, drip campaigns, the credit model, real pricing ranges and where it falls short for outbound and sales teams.
snov-io-review.content:
Quick take: Snov.io bundles email discovery, verification, drip campaigns, mailbox warm-up and a lightweight CRM into one credit-based subscription. That makes it a sensible single tool for a lean team running repeatable outbound. If you mainly need phone numbers, a very large contact database, or deep CRM customisation, a specialist tool will serve you better.

This review is compiled from publicly documented features, provider documentation and independent third-party write-ups. It is not a claim of hands-on testing, and we do not publish lab-style accuracy figures we have not measured ourselves. Where sources disagree, we say so rather than picking the most flattering number.

[affiliate:Explore Snov.io]

What does Snov.io actually do?

Snov.io is a sales prospecting and outreach platform. Rather than one narrow feature, it covers five jobs that most outbound teams otherwise stitch together from three or four subscriptions:

  • Email discovery — a web search, domain search and a Chrome extension that look up professional addresses by name, company or domain.
  • Email verification — real-time and bulk validation of addresses before you send, so you avoid hard bounces.
  • Drip campaigns — multi-step email sequences with scheduling, follow-ups, open and click tracking, and reply detection that stops a sequence when someone answers.
  • Mailbox warm-up — a background process that gradually builds sending reputation on a new mailbox. The number of warm-up slots depends on your plan.
  • A lightweight sales CRM — deals, pipelines and tasks, enough to track a small pipeline without a second tool.

There is also a LinkedIn automation layer, sold as an add-on slot rather than included in the base plans. That distinction matters a lot for budgeting, and we cover it under pricing below.

The Chrome extension is the real entry point

Most people meet Snov.io through its browser extension, which surfaces contact details while you browse a company site or a LinkedIn profile. Independent reviewers consistently describe the extension as included on paid plans and as the fastest way to test whether the underlying data covers your market. A free plan exists, but it is small enough that it works as an interface trial rather than a real pilot.

How many credits does Snov.io use per email?

Snov.io is credit-based, and one credit is not one lead. Finding an address consumes a credit, and verifying the same address consumes another. Independent breakdowns converge on the same arithmetic: a fully checked email costs about two credits.

That single rule changes every plan comparison you will read. A 1,000-credit Starter plan yields roughly 500 find-and-verify operations, not 1,000 usable contacts. If your workflow involves searching broadly, verifying, then enriching, you burn more still.

OperationTypical credit cost
Find a single email address~1 credit
Verify an existing email address~1 credit
Find + verify the same contact~2 credits
Domain or bulk list searchVaries with records returned

Credit costs are documented by third-party sources and can change with plan revisions. Check the provider's current credit documentation before forecasting spend.

[fig:credits-pipeline]

Pricing

Pricing on this page is an approximate snapshot compiled from the third-party sources linked at the bottom. Providers change plans, credit rules and limits frequently, and published figures disagree. Always confirm current pricing on the provider's own pricing page before you buy.

Snov.io sells a free tier plus a ladder of credit tiers. Published monthly figures differ between reviews — one widely cited breakdown lists Starter at $39/month, Pro 5K at $99, Pro 20K at $149 and Pro 50K at $249; another lists Pro 20K at $189 and extends to Pro 100K at $739. Treat the table below as an order-of-magnitude guide, not a quote.

PlanApprox. monthlyCredits / monthEmail recipients / month
Free trial$050100
Starter$30–391,0005,000
Pro 5K$75–995,00010,000
Pro 20K$142–18920,00030,000
Pro 50K$249–36950,00050,000–100,000
Pro 100K$554–739100,000100,000
Enterprise / managed$3,999+CustomCustom

Annual billing is commonly discounted in the region of 20–25% versus monthly, at the cost of paying up front. LinkedIn automation is reported at roughly $69 per slot per month on top of the base plan, which is often the difference between Snov.io looking cheap and looking mid-market.

Three costs that surprise people

  1. Unused credits. Sources disagree on rollover: some say unused credits expire at the end of the billing month, others describe limited rollover. Assume they expire, and size your plan to actual monthly usage.
  2. Double-charging for quality. Because verification costs a credit, being careful about list hygiene is not free — you pay twice per verified contact.
  3. Add-ons. LinkedIn slots and any extra sending capacity sit outside the headline price.

Strengths

  • One workflow, one bill. Finding, verifying, sequencing and tracking in a single interface removes a lot of context-switching for a small team.
  • Verification is built in, not bolted on. Being able to check an address at the point of capture is genuinely better than exporting a list to a separate verifier later.
  • Reply detection and campaign logic. Sequences stop when someone replies, which prevents the most embarrassing outbound mistake.
  • Free tier is real. Fifty credits will not run a campaign, but it will tell you whether the data covers your niche.
  • Broad integration list. HubSpot, Salesforce, Pipedrive, Zapier, Make and Gmail integrations are documented, so it slots into an existing stack.

Limitations

  • Accuracy varies by market. Third-party reviews report overall verification accuracy around 97% and note that quality differs by industry and region. That is respectable, not exceptional, and every finder performs worst in exactly the niches that are hardest to source.
  • The credit model is harder to forecast than flat seats. Finance teams dislike usage-based billing that spikes in a heavy prospecting month.
  • Phone data is not the strength. Snov.io is email-first. If direct dials are core to your motion, a phone-specialist provider is the better primary tool.
  • CRM is genuinely lightweight. It tracks deals, but teams with complex pipelines end up back in HubSpot or Pipedrive.
  • Warm-up is not deliverability. Mailbox warm-up helps reputation; it does not fix missing SPF, DKIM and DMARC records, a badly segmented list, or copy that reads like spam.
  • Jack of several trades. Dedicated verifiers tend to offer deeper tooling, such as API and SDK access for verification at scale, which an all-in-one suite does not match.

Who should choose Snov.io

If you are…Verdict
A solo founder or freelancer doing 200–1,000 contacts a monthGood fit. One subscription replaces a finder plus a verifier plus a sequencer.
A 2–10 person agency running repeatable client outreachStrong fit, but model the credit burn per client before committing to a tier.
A recruiter sourcing candidatesReasonable, provided the candidate niches you work are well covered by the database.
A team that lives on direct-dial phone numbersNot the right primary tool. Pair an email tool with a phone-specialist provider.
An enterprise with complex pipeline requirementsNot a fit as a CRM. Use it as a data and sequencing layer only.

How Snov.io compares to the obvious alternatives

Apollo.io leads with a reported 275M+ contact database plus sequences and a dialer, priced per seat. Hunter.io is a focused, non-per-seat email finder with a separate verification pool. Lusha is phone-first enrichment for LinkedIn workflows. Each has a dedicated comparison on this site:

  • Snov.io vs Hunter.io — all-in-one workflow versus a focused email finder.
  • Snov.io vs Apollo.io — credit-based suite versus the largest prospecting database.
  • Snov.io vs Lusha — email workflow versus phone-number accuracy.
  • All Snov.io alternatives compared.

How we researched this review

We read the provider's own product and pricing documentation, then cross-checked every factual claim against independent third-party reviews and published pricing breakdowns, all linked below. We did not run a paid account, and we do not present any number as a result of our own testing. Where two credible sources disagree — pricing tiers and credit rollover, most often — we show the range instead of choosing a side. Read our full research methodology.

Verdict

Snov.io earns its place as a default all-in-one for small outbound teams because it removes tool sprawl, and the built-in verification genuinely improves list hygiene at the point of capture. Go in with your eyes open about two things: credits are consumed roughly twice per finished contact, and the plan ladder is priced so that heavy months push you up a tier. If you can live inside those constraints, it is a coherent package. If your motion depends on phones or a very large searchable database, start elsewhere and add Snov.io only for sequencing.

[affiliate:Check Snov.io pricing]

Sources

  • Fullenrich — Snov.io pricing breakdown: plans, credits, per-credit cost
  • MentionAgent — Snov.io pricing: annual vs monthly, hidden costs
  • Mystrika — Snov.io review: features, pros, cons, plan table
  • EmailValidationTool — Snov.io review: verification accuracy and limitations
  • Miniloop — database size comparisons across email finders

faq.q: Is Snov.io free to try?
faq.a: Yes. There is a free tier with a monthly credit allowance of around 50 credits and roughly 100 email recipients, with no card required. That is enough to check data coverage in your market but not enough to run a real campaign.

faq.q: How many credits does it take to find and verify one email?
faq.a: Independent breakdowns put it at about two credits: roughly one to find the address and roughly one to verify it. A 1,000-credit plan therefore yields about 500 fully verified contacts.

faq.q: Do unused Snov.io credits roll over?
faq.a: Sources disagree. Several reviews state that unused credits expire at the end of the billing period, while others describe limited rollover on some plans. Plan for expiry and confirm the current rule with the provider.

faq.q: Is Snov.io good for phone numbers?
faq.a: It is email-first. Phone data is available but is not the platform strength compared with phone-specialist providers such as Lusha or the dialer built into Apollo.io.

faq.q: Does Snov.io replace a CRM?
faq.a: It includes a lightweight sales CRM for deals, pipelines and tasks. Teams with complex pipeline or reporting requirements generally keep HubSpot, Pipedrive or Salesforce and use Snov.io for data and sequencing.

snov-io-pricing.title: Snov.io Pricing 2026: Plans and Cost per Lead
snov-io-pricing.description: Snov.io pricing explained: what each credit tier costs, why one lead costs two credits, annual vs monthly rates, add-ons and the hidden costs to model.
snov-io-pricing.content:
Quick take: Snov.io looks inexpensive at the entry tier and gets progressively cheaper per credit as you climb. The catch is that a usable lead costs about two credits, and the things people actually want — LinkedIn automation, extra recipients — are priced or limited separately.

This page is an independent pricing guide compiled from third-party sources linked at the bottom. It is not an official quote. Providers change plans and credit rules without notice, and published figures already disagree between reviewers. Verify on the provider's pricing page before purchasing.

The plan ladder at a glance

PlanApprox. monthlyApprox. annual (per month)Credits / moRecipients / mo
Free$0$050100
Starter$30–39~$301,0005,000
Pro 5K$75–99~$755,00010,000
Pro 20K$142–189~$14220,00030,000
Pro 50K$249–369~$27750,00050,000
Pro 100K$554–739~$554100,000100,000

Different reviewers publish different monthly figures for the same tiers, which is itself a useful signal: treat any single number as indicative. The shape of the ladder is consistent — each step roughly triples credits for well under double the price.

Cost per verified lead, worked out

The headline price tells you almost nothing. What matters is cost per contact you can actually email. Because finding and verifying each consume a credit, divide the plan price by half its credit allowance:

PlanCreditsVerified leads (@2 credits)Approx. cost per verified lead
Starter ($39)1,000~500~$0.08
Pro 5K ($99)5,000~2,500~$0.04
Pro 20K ($189)20,000~10,000~$0.02
Pro 50K ($369)50,000~25,000~$0.015
[fig:cost-per-lead]

That is the core insight of Snov.io pricing: the entry plan has a cost per lead roughly five times higher than the largest tier. If your list building is a one-off experiment, Starter is fine. If prospecting is a permanent function, staying on Starter is expensive in a way the invoice never shows.

Annual versus monthly

Annual billing is widely reported at roughly 20–25% below the monthly rate. On a Pro 5K plan that is a meaningful saving, but it converts a flexible monthly tool into an up-front commitment. The honest test: if you have run two consecutive months of outbound and expect to keep running, annual pays for itself. If you are still validating whether outbound works for you, pay monthly and accept the premium.

The four costs outside the plan price

1. LinkedIn automation slots

Reported at approximately $69 per slot per month. A three-person team that wants LinkedIn automation is adding roughly $207/month to the plan — often more than the base subscription itself.

2. Expiring credits

Most sources state that unused credits do not roll over. Budgeting for 100% utilisation and then using 60% means you paid for 40% of nothing. Size the tier to your real monthly average, not your peak month.

3. Recipient limits

Credit allowance and sending allowance are separate. The Starter plan covers 5,000 recipients, so a cheap plan can still cap a campaign that generates more leads than it can email.

4. Warm-up slots

Warm-up mailbox capacity is plan-limited on lower tiers (commonly three mailboxes on Starter, effectively unlimited higher up). Scaling sending domains before you scale the plan creates a bottleneck.

When to move up a tier

  • Stay put if you finish two months with credits left over.
  • Move up one tier if you exhaust credits before the 20th of the month — running dry mid-month means the tool stops exactly when your campaign needs it.
  • Move up two tiers if you are also near the recipient cap; upgrading for credits alone while hitting the send ceiling is wasted money.
  • Reconsider the tool if more than half your budget goes to LinkedIn slots. At that point you are paying for an automation product with an email tool attached.

Is it good value?

Compared with buying a finder, a verifier and a sequencer separately, a single mid-tier plan is usually cheaper and administratively simpler. Compared with a per-seat all-in-one like Apollo.io, Snov.io is cheaper for one or two users and can be more expensive for a five-person team, because Apollo's cost scales with seats while Snov.io's scales with volume. The crossover depends entirely on whether your bottleneck is people or contacts.

See the head-to-heads for the arithmetic: vs Hunter.io, vs Apollo.io, and vs Lusha. Full feature analysis is in our Snov.io review.

  • Cleanlist — per-seat versus per-account pricing analysis

faq.q: How much does Snov.io cost per month?
faq.a: Reported pricing starts around $30–39/month for the Starter plan with 1,000 credits, rising through roughly $75–99 for 5,000 credits, $142–189 for 20,000, and $249–369 for 50,000. Annual billing is typically 20–25% cheaper than monthly.

faq.q: Why is the real cost per lead higher than the plan price suggests?
faq.a: Because a finished contact costs about two credits, one to find and one to verify. Dividing plan price by half the credit allowance gives a better estimate: roughly $0.08 per verified lead on Starter versus about $0.015 on the largest tiers.

faq.q: Does annual billing save money?
faq.a: Yes, typically 20–25% versus paying monthly. It only makes sense once you have a couple of months of consistent usage behind you, because it converts a cancellable subscription into an up-front commitment.

faq.q: Does Snov.io charge credits for email verification?
faq.a: Yes. Verification is a separate billable action from finding, at roughly one credit per address. Snov.io's own knowledgebase states that valid and invalid results are charged, while unknown (yellow) results are not charged.

faq.q: How much is Snov.io LinkedIn automation?
faq.a: LinkedIn automation is a paid add-on rather than part of the base plan, reported at approximately $69 per slot per month. On a three-person team that can exceed the cost of the subscription itself.

faq.q: Are there extra costs beyond the subscription?
faq.a: LinkedIn automation is reported at about $69 per slot per month, and warm-up mailbox slots and monthly recipient limits vary by tier. Unused credits may expire monthly, which is effectively a cost if you under-use the plan.

snov-io-alternatives.title: 7 Snov.io Alternatives Compared (2026)
snov-io-alternatives.description: The best Snov.io alternatives compared on database size, accuracy, pricing model and outreach features, with clear guidance on which fits your workflow.
snov-io-alternatives.content:
Quick take: Snov.io is strongest when you want finding, verification and sequencing under one subscription. You only need an alternative if your bottleneck is database size (Apollo), phone numbers (Lusha), pure email-finding simplicity (Hunter), or sending infrastructure at volume (Instantly).

Every tool below is described from its own public documentation and independent third-party comparisons linked at the bottom. Reported database sizes and accuracy figures vary between sources; where they conflict we give a range.

The short list

ToolBest forApprox. entry priceReported coverage
Apollo.ioOne platform for data, sequences and dialer$49–59 / user / mo275M+ contacts
Hunter.ioSimple domain-based email finding$34 / mo~107M–200M addresses
LushaPhone-first LinkedIn enrichment$29–39 / user / mo45M–100M contacts
InstantlyCold email sending infrastructure at volumeSeparate sending plans~280M contacts (reported)
Skrapp.ioLinkedIn-based list building with exportFree tier, paid from ~$34LinkedIn-centric
DropcontactEU-focused enrichment and GDPR compliancePer-credit plansEU-weighted
Snov.ioAll-in-one suite with built-in verification$30–39 / mo260M+ contacts (reported)

Prices and coverage figures are approximate and assembled from the cited third-party comparisons. Confirm current details with each provider.

1. Apollo.io — the database play

Apollo is the default alternative for teams whose problem is finding enough of the right people. Reported coverage sits at 275M+ contacts with firmographic filters, technology stack data and funding signals. Unlike Snov.io, it includes sequences and a dialer on the entry plan, and it prices per seat rather than by credit volume.

The trade-off is accuracy. Independent comparisons report email accuracy around 73%, below what focused finders claim. You are trading precision for breadth and for a single platform that does data, outreach and calling. Read the full Snov.io vs Apollo comparison.

2. Hunter.io — the simple finder

Hunter does one thing: find and verify email addresses, mostly by company domain. Its pricing is per account with a shared credit pool, so adding team members costs nothing extra — a structural advantage over per-seat competitors for a five-person team.

It is not a prospecting database. There is no searchable person index and no phone data, and outreach is basic. If your workflow is "I have a list of target companies, get me the right address at each," Hunter is frequently the fastest path. Read the full Snov.io vs Hunter.io comparison.

3. Lusha — the phone-number specialist

Lusha exists for one click: pull a verified mobile number or direct dial from a LinkedIn profile into your CRM. Reported coverage is smaller (45M–100M depending on source), and its database is deliberately phone-weighted. If your motion includes calling, Lusha is a better primary source than Snov.io for that specific job. Read the full Snov.io vs Lusha comparison.

4. Instantly — sending infrastructure, not a full suite

Instantly is built around deliverability at volume: many sender accounts, automatic warm-up, unified inbox and campaign rotation. It is a different layer of the stack. Teams often run Apollo or Hunter for data and Instantly for sending, rather than expecting one tool to do both well.

5. Skrapp.io — LinkedIn list building

Skrapp focuses on extracting contacts from LinkedIn and Sales Navigator, with bulk export and a free allowance. Its verification accuracy is claimed to be high, but independent reviewers note the same limitation every finder has: coverage thins out in niche segments.

6. Dropcontact — the European compliance choice

Dropcontact is oriented around European data protection practice, deriving and verifying professional addresses with a documented legal basis. If your business depends on GDPR defensibility in the EU, that positioning can matter more than raw coverage.

Which one should you pick?

Your situationBest first choiceWhy
One person, limited budget, needs finder + sequencerSnov.ioOne subscription covers discovery, verification and drip campaigns
Team of five on a budget, email onlyHunter.ioPer-account pricing with a shared credit pool, no per-seat fees
Need the biggest searchable databaseApollo.ioReported 275M+ contacts with strong filtering
Outbound includes cold callingLusha + a data sourcePhone accuracy is the differentiator
Sending heavily across many domainsInstantly + a data toolWarm-up and inbox rotation are the core product
EU customers, compliance-sensitiveDropcontactDocumented legal basis for EU data

What to check before switching

  1. Run the same 20 prospects through both tools. Coverage is niche-specific; a demo deck cannot tell you whether your market is indexed.
  2. Compare cost per verified contact, not per credit. A cheaper credit that needs two or three attempts is not cheaper.
  3. Check the pricing axis. Credit-based suites get expensive with volume; per-seat suites get expensive with headcount.
  4. Check renewals and refund terms. Annual discounts are only a discount if you stay.

Start with the full Snov.io review or the pricing breakdown if you are deciding whether to stay.

Sources

  • Fundraise Insider — Lusha alternatives ranked by pricing and data quality
  • Puzzle Inbox — Lusha vs Apollo vs Hunter head-to-head
  • Cleanlist — Hunter vs Apollo feature and pricing comparison

faq.q: What is the best free Snov.io alternative?
faq.a: Apollo.io is generally cited as having the most usable free tier, including a monthly credit allowance and access to sequencing. Hunter.io offers 25 searches per month free, and Lusha has a small free credit allowance. All are limited enough to be evaluation tools rather than production plans.

faq.q: Is Apollo.io better than Snov.io?
faq.a: It depends on your bottleneck. Apollo has a far larger searchable database and includes a dialer, but reported email accuracy is lower and pricing is per seat. Snov.io is cheaper for one or two users and includes verification in the same workflow.

faq.q: Which alternative is best for phone numbers?
faq.a: Lusha, because direct dials and mobiles are its core product rather than a secondary data type. Many teams pair Lusha with an email-first tool rather than replacing one with the other.

faq.q: Can I use two tools together?
faq.a: Yes, and many teams do: one source for data, another for sending. A common pairing is Apollo or Hunter for contact data plus Instantly for multi-domain sending infrastructure.

snov-io-vs-hunter-io.title: Snov.io vs Hunter.io (2026): Which Wins?
snov-io-vs-hunter-io.description: Snov.io vs Hunter.io compared on pricing model, credit costs, email coverage, verification and outreach, with a verdict for freelancers and small teams.
snov-io-vs-hunter-io.content:
Quick take: Hunter.io is the better pure email finder and its per-account pricing is cheaper for teams that only need addresses. Snov.io costs more but bundles verification, drip campaigns and a CRM. If you need to find, check and email in one place, Snov.io wins; if you already have sending software, Hunter wins on focus and price.

Figures below are approximate and compiled from the independent sources listed at the bottom of the page. Database sizes, accuracy claims and prices change frequently, and published figures often disagree between reviewers. Verify with each provider before you buy.

The one-line difference

Hunter answers "what is this person's email address?" Snov.io answers "what is this person's email address, is it deliverable, and can I run a four-step campaign to them?" That is a product-scope difference, not a quality difference, and it determines which one you should buy.

Feature comparison

CapabilitySnov.ioHunter.io
Email finder (name / domain search)YesYes — domain-first strength
Email verificationYes, credits shared with findingYes, separate verification credit pool
Searchable prospect databaseYes, reported 260M+ contactsNo — domain lookup, not a person index
Phone numbersLimitedNo
Drip campaigns / sequencesYes, built inBasic campaigns only
Mailbox warm-upYes, slots by planNo
Sales CRMYes, lightweightNo
Chrome extensionYesYes
API accessYesYes
Pricing axisCredit volumePer account, shared pool
Free tier~50 credits/month25 searches, 50 verifications/month
Approx. entry price$30–39 / month$34 / month (annual)

Pricing, and why the two models diverge

This is where the comparison actually gets decided. Hunter charges per account and lets everyone share the credit pool, so a five-person team pays the same as one person. Snov.io charges for credit volume, which is independent of headcount.

ScenarioSnov.ioHunter.io
Solo user, ~500 verifications/monthStarter, ~$39/moStarter, ~$34/mo
Team of 5, 5,000 searches/monthPro 5K, ~$99/mo totalGrowth, ~$104/mo total
Team of 10, same volumePro 5K, ~$99/mo totalGrowth, ~$104/mo total
Heavy volume, 20,000/monthPro 20K, ~$189/moHigher tier, confirm pricing

Because neither tool charges per seat, both are structurally cheaper than Apollo for small teams. The difference is granularity: Snov.io's entry plan has a high cost per verified lead — about $0.08 once you account for two credits per contact — while its larger tiers drop to roughly $0.015. Hunter's credit pool is shared per account, which flattens cost as you add people.

One asymmetry worth knowing: Snov.io's verification draws from the same credit pool as finding, so being careful about list hygiene has a visible marginal cost. Hunter keeps verification credits in a separate pool, so testing a list does not eat the budget you reserved for discovery.

Data coverage

Reported coverage figures vary widely between sources — Hunter is described as indexing somewhere between roughly 107M and 200M addresses, while Snov.io is reported at 260M+ contacts. Do not treat those numbers as comparable: Hunter counts email addresses discovered by pattern matching across domains, while Snov.io's figure counts people in a searchable database. They are different units measuring different things.

The practical test is the same for both: run 20 of your real target prospects through each free tier and count how many come back correct. Coverage in your specific market matters far more than a global total.

Accuracy

Independent comparisons put Hunter's pattern-based email accuracy around 85%, with a confidence score attached to each result so you can prioritise. Snov.io's verification accuracy is reported in the region of 97% for the verification step. Note carefully that these are not the same measurement — one is about finding the right address, the other about correctly classifying deliverability — so they should not be read as a scoreboard.

Which workflow suits which tool

Choose Hunter.io if…

  • You already have sending software and only need addresses.
  • Your prospecting starts from target company domains rather than a person database.
  • You want a large shared credit pool without per-seat maths.
  • You value a confidence score on every result over bundled extras.

Choose Snov.io if…

  • You want one subscription instead of a finder plus a verifier plus a sequencer.
  • Built-in warm-up and reply detection matter to you.
  • You want a lightweight CRM where the leads land.
  • You prospect by person as well as by company.

Verdict

For a team that already has outreach tooling, Hunter.io is the more honest purchase: cheaper, focused, and good at the one job. For a solo operator or small agency starting from nothing, Snov.io's bundle usually costs less than assembling the equivalent stack, and the built-in verification prevents the specific mistake that ruins cold email — sending to addresses nobody checked. Neither is a mistake; buying both would be.

faq.a: Neither is better in the abstract. Hunter.io is a focused, cheaper email finder with per-account pricing and a separate verification pool. Snov.io bundles verification, drip campaigns, warm-up and a CRM in one subscription. Choose based on whether you need a finder or a full outreach workflow.

faq.q: Which is cheaper for a small team?
faq.a: Both avoid per-seat fees, so both beat per-user competitors for small teams. Hunter is typically a little cheaper at entry level and its credit pool is shared across the account, while Snov.io becomes better value per contact at higher credit tiers.

faq.a: No. Hunter is a domain-based email finder with pattern matching and verification, not a searchable person database like Apollo or Snov.io. If you need to filter by title, industry or headcount, you need a different tool.

faq.a: Comparisons report Hunter pattern-based accuracy around 85% with a confidence score, while Snov.io reports about 97% on its verification step. Those measure different things — finding the right address versus classifying deliverability — so they are not directly comparable.

snov-io-vs-apollo.title: Snov.io vs Apollo.io (2026): Database vs Workflow
snov-io-vs-apollo.description: Snov.io vs Apollo.io compared: 260M vs 275M contacts, email accuracy, per-seat vs credit pricing, sequencing, dialer and which suits solo founders versus SDR teams.
snov-io-vs-apollo.content:
Quick take: Apollo wins on database size, filtering and built-in calling. Snov.io wins on cost for one or two users and on verification accuracy within the same workflow. If your problem is finding enough of the right people, Apollo. If your problem is running a clean, cheap outbound process, Snov.io.

Figures below are approximate and compiled from the independent sources listed at the bottom of the page. Database sizes, accuracy claims and prices change frequently, and published figures often disagree between reviewers. Verify with each provider before you buy.

Scope: a database versus a workflow

Apollo is a prospecting database with an outreach layer on top. You filter 275M+ contacts by title, industry, headcount, technology and funding signals, save a list, and push it into sequences. Snov.io starts from a specific person or company and works outward: find the address, verify it, run a drip campaign, log the deal.

That difference decides most of this comparison before you reach the pricing table. Apollo is built to answer "who should I contact?" Snov.io is built to answer "how do I reach this person reliably?"

Feature comparison

CapabilitySnov.ioApollo.io
Reported database260M+ contacts275M+ contacts
Searchable person databaseYes, less central to the productYes — the core product
Firmographic / technographic filtersLimitedExtensive
Intent and funding signalsNoYes
Email verificationBuilt inBasic, periodic
Drip campaigns / sequencesYesYes, more advanced
Built-in dialer / callingNoYes
Phone numbersLimitedYes
Mailbox warm-upYesLimited
CRMLightweight built-inLightweight built-in
Reported email accuracy~97% on verification step~73% overall
Pricing axisCredit volumePer seat
Free tier~50 credits/monthMonthly credit allowance
Approx. entry price$30–39 / month$49–59 / user / month

Pricing: seats versus credits

Apollo charges per user, so cost rises with headcount and stays flat with volume. Snov.io charges for credits, so cost rises with volume and stays flat with headcount. This produces a clean crossover:

ScenarioSnov.ioApollo.io
Solo founder, moderate volumeStarter ~$39/moBasic ~$49–59/mo
Two-person teamStarter ~$39/mo~$98–118/mo
Five-person teamPro 5K ~$99/mo~$245–295/mo
Adding a sixth repNo changeAdds another seat
Doubling contact volumeMove up a credit tierNo change

For a team of one or two, Snov.io is usually the cheaper way to get finder + verifier + sequencer. For a five-person SDR team, Apollo's per-seat model is often competitive because you get a much larger database and a dialer in the same subscription — provided you can tolerate the accuracy trade-off.

Accuracy is the hidden variable

Independent comparisons report Apollo email accuracy around 73%, materially below focused finders. Breadth has a cost: a 275M-record database inevitably contains more stale records. Snov.io's verification step is reported at roughly 97%, but that measures how well it classifies deliverability, not how often the address it found belongs to the right person.

The practical implication is important. With Apollo, budget for a verification step — either Apollo's built-in check or a third-party verifier — before sending at volume. With Snov.io, that step is already inside the workflow, at the cost of roughly one extra credit per contact.

Deliverability and sending

Snov.io includes mailbox warm-up with slots limited by plan, which is useful if you are starting with a domain that has no sending reputation. Apollo's warmth tooling is more limited, and most high-volume teams pair Apollo with a dedicated sender. Neither platform solves the part that actually determines inbox placement: SPF, DKIM and DMARC authentication, list segmentation, and copy that does not trigger filters.

Choose Apollo.io if…

  • You need to build lists from scratch with precise filters.
  • Your motion includes cold calling and you want dialing in the same tool.
  • You have two or more reps and want one shared source of truth.
  • You will verify contacts before sending, rather than trusting the data.

Choose Snov.io if…

  • You are one or two people and per-seat pricing is punitive.
  • You already know who to contact and need reliable addresses.
  • You want verification, warm-up and sequencing without extra tools.
  • Predictable cost matters more than a huge searchable database.

Verdict

These are the two best-value generalists in the category and they fail in opposite directions. Apollo gives you the widest net but asks you to clean the catch yourself. Snov.io gives you a smaller net with a built-in sieve. For a solo operator, that sieve is worth more than the extra records. For a team of three or more doing list-first outbound, Apollo's database and dialer usually outweigh the accuracy penalty.

faq.a: For one or two users Snov.io is usually cheaper because it charges by credit volume rather than per seat. From around three users upward, Apollo can be competitive or cheaper for the same headcount while offering a larger database.

faq.q: Which has the bigger database?
faq.a: Reported figures put Apollo at 275M+ contacts and Snov.io at 260M+, which is close. The meaningful difference is usability: Apollo is built around filtering a searchable database, while Snov.io is built around looking up specific people and domains.

faq.q: Is Apollo data accurate enough to email directly?
faq.a: Independent comparisons report around 73% email accuracy for Apollo, so most teams verify before sending at volume. Skipping verification generally shows up as elevated bounce rates, which damage sender reputation.

faq.q: Does Snov.io have a dialer?
faq.a: No. Snov.io is email-first and its phone data is limited. If calling is part of your process, Apollo includes a dialer, or you pair an email tool with a phone-specialist provider such as Lusha.

snov-io-vs-lusha.title: Snov.io vs Lusha (2026): Email vs Phone Data
snov-io-vs-lusha.description: Snov.io vs Lusha compared on data type, coverage, accuracy, pricing and export rules, and why most outbound teams end up using both rather than choosing one.
snov-io-vs-lusha.content:
Quick take: This is less a head-to-head than a division of labour. Lusha is a phone-number enrichment tool for LinkedIn-style prospecting. Snov.io is an email discovery and outreach suite. If you must pick one, pick based on whether you contact people by email or by phone — and note that Lusha has no sending features at all.

Figures below are approximate and compiled from the independent sources listed at the bottom of the page. Database sizes, accuracy claims and prices change frequently, and published figures often disagree between reviewers. Verify with each provider before you buy.

What each tool is for

Lusha is designed around a single high-value action: while viewing a LinkedIn profile, reveal that person's direct dial or mobile number and push it into your CRM with one click. Its database is deliberately phone-weighted, and its coverage is smaller than email-first platforms.

Snov.io is designed around a process: find an email address, verify it, add the contact to a drip campaign, and track the resulting deal. Its phone data exists but is not the product's centre of gravity.

Feature comparison

CapabilitySnov.ioLusha
Primary data typeProfessional emailDirect dial / mobile phone
Reported coverage260M+ contacts45M–100M contacts (sources vary)
Email findingCore strengthAvailable, secondary
Phone numbersLimitedCore strength
Email verificationBuilt inLimited
Drip campaigns / sequencesYesNo
Mailbox warm-upYesNo
CRMLightweight built-inNo — pushes to your CRM
Chrome extensionYesYes, LinkedIn-first
Pricing axisCredit volumePer seat
Free tier~50 credits/monthSmall monthly credit allowance
Approx. entry price$30–39 / month$29–39 / user / month

Coverage and accuracy

Lusha's reported coverage varies between 45M and 100M contacts depending on the source, which is a reminder of how soft these figures are. Its advantage is not volume but specialisation: mobile and direct-dial data is harder to source than email and Lusha is one of the few providers that treats it as the primary product.

Snov.io's larger reported footprint reflects an email-first index. For phone-heavy workflows, a 260M email database does not compensate for thin dial coverage — a phone number you cannot reach is worth nothing, and that is precisely the gap Lusha fills.

Pricing compared

Lusha prices per user, typically from around $29–39 per user per month, with premium tiers for higher export volumes. Snov.io prices by credit volume, from around $30–39 per month on Starter, and does not charge per seat.

ScenarioSnov.ioLusha
Solo user, email-focusedStarter ~$39/moPro ~$39/user/mo (phone focus)
Three reps needing mobile numbersStarter ~$39/mo — but thin phone data~$117+/mo
Three reps running email campaignsPro 5K ~$99/mo totalNot applicable — no sending
Budget for both jobs~$39–99/moAdd $39+/user/mo

Why most teams use both

Because the two tools answer different questions. A typical stack is an email source plus a phone enrichment layer: Snov.io or Hunter for addresses and sequences, Lusha for dials on the accounts that warrant a call. Combining Snov.io Starter with a single Lusha seat lands around $78–80 per month, which is less than most single-platform upgrades at mid-tier.

What you should avoid is choosing Lusha as your email workflow tool — it has no sequences, no warm-up and no campaign tracking, so you would still need something to send from — or choosing Snov.io as your phone source, where coverage is the weakest part of the product.

Choose Lusha if…

  • Your outbound includes cold calling or SMS as a real channel.
  • You prospect primarily from LinkedIn and want one-click enrichment.
  • You already have sending software and just need contact data.

Choose Snov.io if…

  • Email is your primary channel and you want the whole workflow in one place.
  • You need verification and warm-up alongside discovery.
  • You are one or two people and per-seat pricing adds up quickly.

Verdict

Pick Lusha when the deliverable is a phone number; pick Snov.io when the deliverable is a sent, tracked campaign. For most small teams the correct answer is not a choice at all — the two products barely overlap, and stacking them costs less than most people expect.
